title: I believe that polyamory should be promoted more in media - and that the binary "She Must Choose One" trope is harmful for everyone. CMV
text:
I believe that healthy polyamorous relationships should be held up in society and media, and that it is harmful to imply that a person cannot in any circumstances love two people, or especially that someone (usually female) must choose between Love Interest A and Love Interest B. This is particularly common in young adult oriented romance.

I have to admit that I'm unsure if my view on this can be changed, but I would at least like to understand the other side more.

The way I see it, the media does not really "promote" a type of family unit as a whole. The media generally outputs what we are already. The fact that the media sells the nuclear family because it is the average of what exists. If the average family were a three parent, three child group, that is what the media would show. Think of it more as a mirror of average real families rather than a depiction of what you should idealize.

Additionally, those love stories depict dilemmas as you described because it is something that many people can relate to. That is the way the majority of the world really does work, not just some movie fabrication.

In the real world, most people would have a hard time getting love interest A and B to go along with dating them together. It isn't normal for that to happen. That doesn't make it unhealthy or wrong for it to happen, it's just a situation most people are not comfortable with, and thus audiences would not be able to identify with it and it wouldn't sell.

I don't see how you could interpret the trope as harmful. Even if you think people are only monogamous because they were trained to be, you are simply advocating a new thing to train into people. Displaying the average excludes the lowest number of people. The only way for the media to not exclude any one would be to depict nothing. Promoting an atypical relationship status as ideal alienates the masses, and the media doesn't do that.

Now, if you argue not to promote a new ideal, but rather to reduce negative displays of something atypical, then I am fine with it.

&#8710;

While this didn't change my view completely, it did give me a better idea of what my view actually *is*.

I think part of why people have a hard time getting LIA and LIB to go along with a "V" relationship is that, for a lot of people, poly just isn't an idea they've ever been exposed to in a non-negative way. Growing up my only experience with poly in *any* form was either church history (I grew up Mormon, so it had to be ordained by God and "We don't practice that anymore." and for the most part polygamy was viewed very negatively), or "Those weird crazy people" - from brief encounters with members of various FLDS sects.

I don't believe that the trope itself is harmful - some people, perhaps most, prefer monogamy as their relationship model, and that's totally fine. Of course they may have to choose between two or more potential partners. That is also just fine by me.

I think that the trope being *the only acceptable option available* is the harmful part.

So yes; I don't argue that polyamory is the ideal solution for all the worlds problems - or even any of them. I would just like to see it offered as a solution in media more often, and for polyamorous relationships to be shown as a viable, healthy alternative to monogamy (Big Love shows a polygamous family, but I would not consider the relationships shown to be healthy or viable, for example).

Monogamy is not harmful and polyamory hardly seems preferable.  I imagine that anyone who has had a stepparent and/or stepsiblings has wondered which was the preferred family line.  That kind of insecurity-fostering internal debate hardly seems healthy.

Although it might be worth considering that "wondering which is the preferred family line" is an artifact from monogamous model since it tells you there is *supposed* to be a nuclear family of that sort, and so naturally you wonder if you are actually part of it.  If the prevailing model were polyamorous though, where the norm was that a family was not so concentrated on two people, then it's entirely possible that those sorts of questions would cease to even make sense.

Just to clarify -

Harmful for everyone?

In all circumstances? 

Please don't read any further, if, as I'm convinced, that's not the case. 

I can only disagree with you, if you meant we must portray everyone as poly. For many of us, there must be a choice made, even if we accept that there are others who are hurt by our limitations. 

I'm perfectly okay with my poly partners sleeping with other people. But asking me to do the same was the reason I ended my two longest relationships. It felt like a betrayal, and an abandonment...and I don't know why. My fantasy life isn't monogamous. I'm not immune to temptation. I've flipped traditional values the bird so many times that it probably counts as fingering at this point.

But I'd instinctively claw the eyes out of anyone who tried to force a sexual/romantic encounter on me, when I'm with someone else. Or if I couldn't stop it, just spend the entire time not feeling anything, being far away from it all, waiting for it to end... 

And you can't imagine the rush of my partner defending me from others. I'm terrified of it. It's like flying on a dragon, it's like being crowned royalty, and it's so wonderful that I will never willingly place myself in a position to become addicted to it.

If I could change all of this, I would be much happier...but I suspect my efforts to try to become something I'm not weren't that much different from the polyamorous woman who amputates parts of herself in order to conform to someone else's design. For her, it's like losing limbs. For me, like losing my skin.

>Just to clarify -

>Harmful for everyone?

>In all circumstances?

Oh, certainly not.

I think that the current way that monogamy is presented - that is, as the only option in all cases - is harmful. But certainly people should be able to choose for themselves how they want to live their lives.

Jealousy is a dangerous thing, and I would postulate that there are few (if any) polyamorous relationships where everyone in them is completely happy.  Even if there are some, they are much rarer than standard, two-person relationships, and of course, media must appeal to the masses in order to get money, the driving cause of almost everything.

I would like to ask that you define "completely happy" - because I would argue that very few relationships at all are *completely* happy.

In my experience with the poly community, I've noticed that polyamorous partners seem to be much more open regarding dissatisfaction within a relationship. If a partner is feeling unhappy about something in the relationship they are often encouraged to look outside for something different, that would fill that need.

As an example from my life - I am really rather a romantic. I love being woo-ed. But my Boyfriend isn't the type of person to buy random sweet little gifts just to make me feel special. He would if I asked him to, but it would take a lot of time and energy to keep reminding him - and then it wouldn't be as special. Currently I don't have a second partner, but I imagine that s/he would enjoy doing those little acts of romance, since it is a place where I do occasionally feel unfulfilled.

Right now I fill that by being the romantic partner, and surprising Boyfriend with flowers and small gifts every so often.

As for jealousy: I would argue that jealousy is a problem in all relationships if and when it comes up. I believe that jealousy, like any other problem within a relationship, can only be confronted by the partners talking about it and coming to a conclusion. The important thing to realize about jealousy specifically, is that it is coming from *somewhere*. Identifying why you (general you) feel jealous about something is the first step to overcoming it. I would also argue that polyamorous couples have more resources for coping with jealousy, simply given the vast amount of poly blogs and websites devoted to that specific issue.

Are you suggesting that the poly community dealing with jealousy is larger than the standard relationship jealousy resource pool?  I would disagree on that issue, I'm sure there are numbers for it somewhere.

Ok, I would agree that few relationships are completely happy.

However, my point stands that the media, to perform its role in the world, must pander to the masses, which, at least now, consist of mainly two-person couples or singles hoping to be one of those couples.

>Are you suggesting that the poly community dealing with jealousy is larger than the standard relationship jealousy resource pool?

I'm merely suggesting that jealousy is looked at as a problem to be solved within the poly community, where - in my experience/observations - outside of the community, at least some jealousy is considered healthy and desirable in a relationship (for example: It seems to be expected for a girl to become jealous or upset if her boyfriend looks at another woman for too long).

I suppose that's fair, I don't really know much about the poly community, perhaps jealousy is handled in a different way.

Do you object to my claim that the media's job is to give the people what they want, and that what most people want to see in a romantic film of any type is usually the "she / he must choose one?"

The gripe I have with your view in this comment is that it seems like you are taking for granted what it means to be a S.O./partner to someone.

> Currently I don't have a second partner, but I imagine that s/he would enjoy doing those little acts of romance, since it is a place where I do occasionally feel unfulfilled.

And how would your current boyfriend feel if he knew that part of your romantic fulfillment was coming from someone other than him? I'm not sure that jealousy is the only volatile factor here. He might feel that sustaining a relationship with you is not worth it if he is not able to provide all of the emotional support and romance you need, even if you two work on it together. And I would agree with him.

I think that the point of relationships is to find a person to support you. If you are "in a relationship" with multiple people and can always just add another person to your romantic life every time a new problem arises, then you are diluting the obligation and commitment that you really have toward each of these "partners". If you can't work out your problems with one partner and have to go to an outside source to fulfill the need, then maybe that one partner is not right for you at all and you need to simply seek a new partner who is more willing to fulfill your needs and work on problems with you.

>And how would your current boyfriend feel if he knew that part of your romantic fulfillment was coming from someone other than him?

Honestly he looks at it as the same as any relationship I have that doesn't involve him: He's happy that I'm happy, and he'd be happy that I was getting what I needed out of life.

>He might feel that sustaining a relationship with you is not worth it if he is not able to provide _all of the emotional support and romance you need_, even if you two work on it together.

Italics mine, because that's the part I want to address. Neither Boyfriend nor myself believes that he can *ever* fulfill all of my emotional and romantic needs - or that I can fulfill all of his.  Honestly we have a pretty awesome relationship, and it's not something either of us would give up without one hell of a fight.

The rest I would go into, but it's not the topic of discussion, and involves a lot of my own personal beliefs and values. If you'd like me to go on, I will, but I can only type so much tonight.
Look around you.  People have proven highly inept at handling two person relationships.  Why would adding one or more additional personalities to the mix be a good idea?

I'm probably not very qualified to answer this, actually. I've surrounded myself with people who have very functional, happy mono and poly relationships, and in my little circle of acquaintances, there is very little relationship drama.

I think that one of the big issues with how relationships are shown in media is there's so very often the plot of "Girl must choose which boy she likes best" - which leads to drama because then the boys are competing for attention and - if and when she does choose one - they're jealous and paranoid that she likes the other guy more.

Since media tends to - either directly or indirectly - write our scripts for real life, that's the same plot I've seen in real dysfunctional relationships. Two partners don't trust each other because there's this fear of "another woman" or "another man". Sure, cheating is possible in a polyamorous relationship, but why would you bother if you could just talk to your partner about it?
Realistically, it's virtually impossible to love two people equally.  Someone will always be the less loved one, and that's a really shitty place to be in if you're #2.
I suspect that the one who is less loved would change with time. Sometimes Person A is the most loved, sometimes Person B is, and that it balances out with time.

> Look around you. People have proven highly inept at handling two person relationships.

Where are we looking?  Are you saying that polyamory is a regular thing that we see people doing all the time?   I've only known 1 person in real life to do it, and they seemed to manage just fine...how many people do you know who've tried it?
I was referring to your standard binary relationship.
Ah my bad.  I misread you.  I thought you were saying people who date two people at once.

Indeed humans, specifically biological males, are not monogamous in nature. Men, psychologically are "cultured" or "trained" to be monogamous. Now, polyamorous relationships do exist, and they have existed throughout human history (and still exist in some communities/countries), but lets not get into that.

The truth of the matter is the globalised culture of the United States and Western Europe places a cultural emphasis on monogamous relationships. More specifically one man and one women. This can be a product of Christianity and its influence on the idea of marriage relationships. The idea of marriage is as much a social as it is legal idea of a partnership between parties, one where at least in the United States does not accept (legally) the partner ship of more than two people (see Reynolds v. United States) as well as homosexual unionships (in a majority of states). Because entering in a legal marriage between more than two people is barred in the United States there is a perception that polyamory is illegal entirely. Perceptions shape world views, and by large many still find the notion of polyamory inherently wrong on moral grounds.

Because of this, there is a cultural identity of what a relationship is. Most people still automatically think a 'romantic partner' refers to your dedicated monogamous partner of the opposite sex (something slowly changing to include homosexual relationships). People will behave to conform to this cultural model, and when confronted by a polyamorous relationship will have to cope with feelings of jealousy and will be faced with changing their perceptions of relationships (quite a difficult task).

Truth be told, there needs to be a shift in the definition of relationships, even more so, a definition in marriage. Until that happens, it's unlikely to change. We are seeing a shift on how relationships are defined. Gay couples are entering the media and laws are being changed. Polyamorous relationships have their own unique problems that prevent them from being discussed or portrayed. I'm not going to talk about healthy relationships, or how polyamory cannot work, but I will say that culturally, it simply is not accepted and built into our cultural identity. It's not a hot topic as gay marriage is, nor is it something I believe will be for a time. The media creates shows that will appeal to an audience, and polyamorous relationships are not part of that cultural identity.

A lot of people are making some claims about polyamory and the cultural roots of the (fairly modern) preference toward monogamous relationships that I feel are either unfounded or irrelevant. I don't know if there are enough rigorous studies to really draw broad conclusions about whether polyamory in modern times is a significantly more or less healthy lifestyle than monogamous relationships on average, but the intuition that monogamy is inherently more stable and less problematic is pretty much necessarily going to be heavily culturally biased by the status quo. I don't think that's a point that anyone really has the background to argue here without it being largely bullshit, myself included, and besides, I happen to agree that there's nothing inherently wrong with polyamory and that it should be more culturally accepted, and don't particularly feel like playing devil's advocate about that.

Fortunately, it's really beside the point. The idea that the media should promote or avoid promoting any set of values in particular, especially with regards to the nature of interpersonal relationships, is the primary problem with your view. Things like sitcoms, romances, myths, and other stories draw inspiration from reality, the imaginations and cultural biases of the authors, and from desire to appeal to certain demographics. 

While it's well-established that fiction and media have an effect on societal norms, they can equally be said to be a product of them, and regulating the messages that can be conveyed is always going to be problematic. As far as efficacy, messages that are far enough from cultural norms, or even favor one side in a dichotomy between competing cultural norms, have to be extremely artfully conveyed to be convincing, and will often result in a backlash if done poorly, especially in an educated society that's aware of the concept of propaganda. And if something is far enough away from what people consider normal, they also might just consider it part of the setting or the premise, and not necessarily something that applies to their situation or that they should really think about.

In addition, I don't necessarily like that media has to be careful about pandering to its audience in order to be financially successful, but it's probably not a phenomenon that's going away anytime soon. Much like nemeses, just wars, and hero's journeys, the standard romantic love triangle isn't a particularly common situation in everyday life (If only because the real world tends to be more complicated than that), but it's a cultural meme that has broad appeal and speaks the language that consumers of fiction are used to. While it may be a valid solution in the real world, having the characters simply decide to enter a polyamorous relationship might seem like a cop-out to said fiction-consumers, or they'll scoff at it for being naive, even if it is equally naive to resolve the love triangle a more typical way.

We can idly say that TV or Movies or popular fiction of some other kind *should* be promoting or discouraging this or that, but ultimately they're mainly going to be responding to the artistic intentions of the creators of the fiction, as well as market pressures acting on what becomes successful. Trying to change that in a widespread way will be heavy-handed no matter how you do it, and probably will not be very effective.

Ultimately, if you think the media should promote polyamorous relationships, I encourage you to go out and write a book, or a TV show, or a movie that does just that. Write a compelling romantic lead whose primary struggle isn't choosing between two love interests, but trying to convince them to reconcile their differences and agree to a polyamorous relationship to the benefit of all. I'm sure it could be made a less boring movie than most formulaic romances these days, so you might even be successful. But my point is that challenging cultural norms through media is going to have to happen from the bottom up, not the top down. Don't think of what the media *should* be doing, because that concept is irrelevant and will go nowhere. Become part of the media and do it.

Just because it is technically possible to have healthy multi-relationships does not change the fact that the vast majority of people are not mature enough to by any even remote stretch of the imagination.
